# Distributed Training and Sharding

Also called: Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting, Multi-GPU 3DGS, Sharded Gaussian Training

## Overview
Distributed Training and Sharding refers to the family of methods that partition the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training and rendering pipeline across multiple GPUs to overcome single-GPU memory limits and accelerate city-scale or high-resolution reconstruction. It solves the problem where the number of Gaussian primitives or the resolution of the scene exceeds the VRAM capacity of a single device. What sets this family apart from its siblings is the specific strategy for distributing the global state (Gaussians) and the workload (pixels/views): [BlitzGS](15088-blitzgs.md) uses index-parity sharding to avoid spatial redundancy; [Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting](16979-distributed-3d-gaussian-splatting.md) focuses on scientific volume data with global gradient synchronization; [Distributed Batched Rendering Loop](18495-distributed-batched-rendering-loop.md) and [Grendel](19770-grendel.md) use dynamic, view-aware all-to-all communication to balance pixel-wise loads; and [Online Image Rendering Placement](19195-online-image-rendering-placement.md) optimizes patch assignment via Integer Linear Programming heuristics.

## Shared principles
The methods in this family share a foundation in 3D Gaussian primitives defined by mean $\mu$, covariance $\Sigma$ (derived from scale $s$ and rotation $q$), opacity $\alpha$, and color/radiance parameters. Rendering involves projecting these 3D primitives to 2D screen space, typically via affine approximation of the projective transformation. The core mathematical operation is the evaluation of the Gaussian density function $P(x|\mu, \Sigma) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x - \mu)\right)$ and alpha blending. Acceleration often relies on tiling the image plane and sorting primitives by depth.

## Subtopics

### [BlitzGS](15088-blitzgs.md)
BlitzGS is a distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework designed to accelerate city-scale reconstruction by reducing the active Gaussian workload at system, model, and view levels. Unlike spatial block partitioning which suffers from cross-block redundancy and imbalanced shards, BlitzGS shards Gaussians across GPUs by index parity and applies importance-based filtering to prune redundant primitives and gate spawns. It achieves nearly an order-of-magnitude faster training time compared to baselines like Momen.GS and CityGS-X while maintaining high reconstruction quality.

### [GS-Cache Inference Framework](15588-gs-cache-inference-framework.md)
GS-Cache is a holistic rendering framework designed to support real-time rendering of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models, specifically targeting city-level scenes. It achieves an average frame rate exceeding 72 FPS at binocular 2K resolution by employing a cache-centric de-redundancy pipeline and elastic parallel scheduling. Unlike native 3DGS or unstructured methods, GS-Cache specifically targets "Structured Gaussian derivation methods" (such as Scaffold-GS and Octree-GS) that use anchors to derive neural Gaussians, addressing the computational bottleneck of the "Gaussian Derivation Stage" which dominates processing time. It sets itself apart from siblings like [BlitzGS](15088-blitzgs.md) and [Grendel](19770-grendel.md) by focusing on inter-frame redundancy elimination in the anchor decoding phase rather than just rasterization acceleration or distributed sharding.

### [Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting](16979-distributed-3d-gaussian-splatting.md)
Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting is a multi-GPU extension of the 3D-GS pipeline designed for scientific visualization, enabling the scalable processing of large datasets that exceed single-GPU memory capacity. It differs from single-GPU baselines by distributing the global point cloud and Gaussian parameters across multiple GPUs, allowing for the reconstruction of scenes with tens of millions of primitives. Unlike [BlitzGS](15088-blitzgs.md) which focuses on inference acceleration, this method specifically addresses the training scalability for high-fidelity isosurface reconstruction from scientific volume data.

### [Distributed Batched Rendering Loop](18495-distributed-batched-rendering-loop.md)
A distributed rendering pipeline that processes camera views in batches, dividing the workload across multiple GPUs to enable high-resolution and large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training and inference that exceeds single-GPU memory limits. It differs from single-GPU rendering by introducing a dynamic strategy phase that maps camera views to GPU tasks, followed by sparse all-to-all communication to distribute Gaussian primitives to the GPUs responsible for rendering specific pixel regions. Unlike methods that process one view at a time, this loop supports batched training using multiple views, improving GPU utilization and scaling rendering quality by increasing the total quantity of Gaussians.

### [Online Image Rendering Placement](19195-online-image-rendering-placement.md)
Online Image Rendering Placement is a distributed training optimization method that dynamically assigns image patches to GPUs at each training iteration to minimize inter-node communication and balance computational load. It distinguishes itself from static partitioning methods by solving an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem online using a fast heuristic solver, allowing it to adapt to the random batch selection inherent in differentiable rendering training.

### [Grendel](19770-grendel.md)
Grendel is a distributed training system for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that partitions parameters and parallelizes computation across multiple GPUs to overcome single-GPU memory constraints in high-resolution and large-scale reconstruction. It distinguishes itself by exploiting mixed parallelism (Gaussian-wise and pixel-wise) and spatial locality to handle dynamic, unbalanced workloads, while supporting batched training with multiple camera views to improve GPU utilization. Unlike systems that rely on dense weight sharding or divide-and-conquer cell partitioning, Grendel uses sparse all-to-all communication to transfer only relevant Gaussians and employs dynamic load balancing to maintain efficiency.

### LS-Gaussian Accelerator Architecture
- **Definition:** A hardware architecture co-designed with the LS-Gaussian algorithm to support workload-aware mapping, featuring a streaming pipeline that allows continuous processing across hardware modules without requiring global synchronization [S1].
- **Step:** The accelerator predicts the workload for each tile based on viewpoint transformation to enable more balanced parallel computation [S1].
- **Comparison:** Unlike naive assignment of tiles to rendering blocks which fails to achieve balanced load distribution, this architecture uses workload prediction to mitigate inter-block idling and intra-block bubbles [S1].

### Spatial Block Partitioning
- **Definition:** Divides the scene into fixed world-space spatial blocks (e.g., uniform grid). Each GPU is bound to a specific block and trains its Gaussians independently [S2, unofficial].
- **Step:** Construct a uniform grid (e.g., 4×5 or 5×6). Assign each block a boundary halo of neighboring Gaussians for cross-block consistency. Train blocks independently across GPUs. During rendering, cameras near block boundaries trigger cross-block visibility overlap and boundary reassignment. Perform a final single-GPU merge to assemble the full scene [S2, unofficial].
- **Pitfall:** Overlapping blocks re-optimize the same surfaces, wasting computation. In a 20-block split, 23.5M Gaussians are optimized but only 5.37M survive merge (77% discarded). Finer partitions increase redundancy and training time with negligible quality gain (<0.2 dB) [S2, unofficial].
- **Number:** On Building (1,920 cameras, 4 GPUs), 86.8% of cameras fall in ≥2 blocks for 20-block partition, and 95.5% for 30-block partition. Wall-clock time for split/make-span/merge reaches 115.6–169.8 min vs 39 min for sharding [S2, unofficial].

### Primitive Sharding (Index-Parity Sharding)
- **Definition:** Distributes a single global Gaussian model across multiple GPUs by assigning Gaussians to ranks based on index parity. Each GPU holds a balanced, scene-wide slice of the model [S2, unofficial].
- **Step:** Assign each Gaussian primitive to a GPU rank using index parity. During rendering, distribute each step through balanced tile allocation across GPUs. Route projected Gaussians to tile owners via all-to-all communication. Train using a single global camera stream. Each camera enters training once per iteration with no cross-block duplication. Only distributed cost is the all-to-all exchange inside each render step [S2, unofficial].
- **Number:** On a 4-GPU setup (Building scene, 1,920 cameras), communication cost for routing projected Gaussians to tile owners is 3–5 ms per iteration, staying under 7% of total iteration time [S2, unofficial].
- **Comparison:** Unlike spatial block partitioning, it eliminates boundary reassignment, cross-block visibility overlap, and the final single-GPU merge step. Storage and per-step rendering remain evenly distributed as GPU count grows [S2, unofficial].

### Naive Offloading
- **Definition:** A CPU offloading strategy for 3DGS training that transfers all Gaussian attributes to CPU memory before rendering, using pinned memory and CPU Adam [S3].
- **Step:** Adopts pre-rendering frustum culling for efficient kernel computation. Trains each batch one image at a time with gradient accumulation to reduce activation memory usage [S3].

## Background
The need for distributed training in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises from the quadratic growth of memory requirements with scene complexity and resolution. Early implementations were limited to single-GPU setups, restricting the scale of reconstructible scenes. The development of distributed methods has been driven by two main applications: large-scale urban reconstruction (e.g., BlitzGS, Grendel) and scientific visualization of volumetric data (e.g., Distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting). Key innovations include moving from spatial partitioning (which causes redundancy) to index-parity sharding (which balances load) [S2, unofficial], and introducing dynamic load balancing to handle the irregular visibility of Gaussians [S1][S2, unofficial]. The field also explores hardware-aware optimizations, such as the LS-Gaussian accelerator, to mitigate hardware stalls caused by workload imbalance [S1].
